title: Explaining Delays & Their Causes Diplomatically
titleEs: Explicar retrasos y sus causas con diplomacia
summary: Explain why something is late without sounding defensive: the Present Perfect Continuous for a cause that is still active (*we've been waiting for the supplier's data since the 2nd*), nouns and passives for the delay itself (*there has been a delay in…*, *has been held up by…*) and hedges that keep the tone professional.
canDo: Explain the cause of a delay with *have been + -ing* and link it to the present consequence.
Turn a blunt cause into diplomatic language: *there has been a delay in…*, *partly*, *it has taken longer than expected*.
Propose a revised date and say what is not affected, in the same message.
Say *as a result* and *held up* as single blocks and reduce *than* to /ðən/.

focus.grammar: Present Perfect Continuous for an active cause (*we've been waiting for…, so…*) · Present Perfect passive (*has been delayed / held up by*) · cause and consequence: because of, due to, owing to, as a result, which is why · hedges: partly, slightly, longer than expected
focus.lexis: fall behind schedule, a setback, push back (a date), slip, be held up by, take longer than expected, get back on track, in the meantime, hit a snag, owing to / due to
focus.afh: linking in as a result / held up / than expected · weak than /ðən/ · stress: a SETback vs set BACK, deLAY, unforeSEEN · -ed in expected /tɪd/

warmup: Think of the last time something you were responsible for was late. What was the real cause, and how did you explain it? Would you explain it the same way to a friend and to a client?

scenario.title: Reporting module: revised date
scenario.context: The reporting module is going to be two weeks late. Ryan writes to Helen Marsh, the client's program director, before she hears it from someone else.
scenario.speaker: ryan
scenario.text: Dear Helen, I'm writing to update you on the reporting module. {{There has been a delay in}} the data-export work: we{{'ve been waiting for}} the supplier's updated data format since the 2nd, and adapting our scripts to it {{has taken longer than expected}}. {{As a result}}, the module {{has slipped}} by about two weeks, from May 23 to June 6. {{In the meantime}}, we{{'ve been testing}} the other four modules with real users, so the overall go-live date is not affected. I'll send you a revised plan by Friday. Best regards, Ryan
scenario.tts: Dear Helen, I'm writing to update you on the reporting module. There has been a delay in the data-export work: we've been waiting for the supplier's updated data format since the second, and adapting our scripts to it has taken longer [than](/ðən/) expected. As a result, the module has slipped by about two weeks, from May twenty-third to June sixth. In the meantime, we've been testing the other four modules with real users, so the overall go-live date is not affected. I'll send you a revised plan by Friday. Best regards, Ryan

organizer.explain: Active cause in the Present Perfect Continuous, an explicit link (*as a result*, *which is why*, *so*), and a present consequence in the Present Perfect Simple or the passive.

questions.q: In *we've been waiting for the supplier's data since the 2nd, so the module has slipped by two weeks*, which part is the cause and which is the consequence? Is the cause still active now, or is it over? How does that affect the way Helen hears the delay?
questions.model: The cause is *we've been waiting for the supplier's data since the 2nd*; the consequence is *the module has slipped by two weeks*. The cause is still active: the team is still waiting, which is why the continuous form is used. Helen hears a delay explained by an ongoing external dependency, not by a finished mistake, so the message reads as an account of the situation rather than as an excuse.
criteria: You identified the cause (*have been waiting*) and the consequence (*has slipped*).
You said the cause is still going on, which is why the continuous form is used.
You linked the choice of form to how the client hears the delay: an ongoing dependency, not a closed error.

questions.q: Look at *has slipped by two weeks*, *hasn't been pushed back* and, from the formal register, *has been held up by a change*. Which forms are active and which are passive? Write the passive pattern, and say what *by* introduces.
questions.model: *Has slipped* is active (Present Perfect Simple: *has + past participle*). *Hasn't been pushed back* and *has been held up by a change* are passive: *has / have + been + past participle*, and *by* introduces the cause, the agent. The passive lets you name the delay without naming a person: the module was held up by a change in the data format, not by Alex.
criteria: You separated the active form (*has slipped*) from the passive ones (*has been pushed back / held up*).
You wrote the passive pattern: *has / have been + past participle*.
You said *by* introduces the cause and that the passive avoids naming a person.

questions.q: Compare *The supplier changed the format and we're late* with *There has been a delay in the export work; adapting the scripts has taken longer than expected, partly because our estimate was optimistic*. What do *there has been a delay*, *longer than expected* and *partly* do to the tone? Where is the line between diplomacy and hiding the truth?
questions.model: *There has been a delay in…* and *it has taken longer than expected* describe the delay as an event, not as somebody's fault; *partly* admits a share of responsibility without exaggerating it. The tone becomes factual and calm, which protects the relationship. The line is simple: the hedges must sit next to the real cause and a revised date (*owing to a change in the supplier's format; revised date 6 June*). Softening without facts is evasion, and clients notice.
criteria: You said these phrases present the delay as an event rather than as blame.
You said *partly* accepts a share of responsibility honestly.
You said diplomatic language still has to state the real cause and a new date.

points: To explain a delay, give the cause that is still active with the Present Perfect Continuous (*we've been waiting for… since…*) and the present consequence with the Present Perfect Simple (*the module has slipped*) or the present (*the export isn't ready yet*).
Link cause and consequence explicitly: *so*, *as a result*, *which is why*, or *because of / due to / owing to* + noun phrase (*because* + clause).
The passive and impersonal nouns keep people out of the sentence: *the module has been held up by a change*, *there has been a delay in the export work*.
Diplomatic language is specific: a hedge (*partly*, *slightly*, *longer than expected*) next to the real cause, what is not affected, and a revised date.
formulas: have / has been + -ing (cause) + so / as a result + have / has + past participle (consequence)
There has been a delay in + noun · has / have been held up by + cause
due to / owing to + noun phrase · because / which is why + clause
rule.note: Spanish often states the cause bluntly and in the present (*es que el proveedor cambió el formato y vamos tarde*). In English, *there has been a delay in…* + a hedged cause + a revised date reads as professional, not as evasive.

phonetics.intro: Al explicar un retraso usas bloques fijos que el oído nativo espera enlazados: *as a result* suena «a-za-ri-ZALT» y *held up*, «hel-DAP». También se debilitan las palabras funcionales: *than* en *longer than expected* se reduce a /ðən/. Y dos acentos que el español coloca en otra sílaba: *delay* y *setback*.

items.meaning: because of what was just said; used to introduce a consequence

alerts.text: La z de *as* se une a *a* («a-za») y el bloque sigue sin pausa hasta *result*: «a-za-ri-ZALT». Cuatro palabras, un solo golpe de voz.
*Result* lleva el acento en la última sílaba, «ri-ZALT», con s sonora /z/ (un zumbido). No «RE-sult».
*A* es una schwa /ə/ brevísima, y *as* queda corto, casi /əz/, en habla rápida.

example.speaker: priya
example.text: As a result, the date has slipped by two weeks.

alerts.text: La d de *held* pasa a *up*: «hel-DAP», no «held / ap». Es la d la que enlaza.
La h es una aspiración suave, nunca una jota. Y la d final se pronuncia: sin ella no hay enlace.
/ʌ/ de *up* es una a corta y relajada, «ap», no «up» con u.

example.speaker: oliver
example.text: The export has been held up by a change in the data format.

items.meaning: more than people had planned or predicted

alerts.text: *Than* casi siempre es débil: /ðən/, «dhan», con schwa. Ni «dan» ni «zan» ni «dán» con vocal plena.
La n de *than* enlaza con la vocal de *expected*: «dha-nik-SPEK-tid».
*Expected* termina en /tɪd/: tras una t, el sufijo -ed añade una sílaba, «tid». Compara con *pushed* /t/ y *slipped* /t/, sin sílaba extra.

example.speaker: alex
example.text: It has taken longer than expected to adapt the scripts.
example.tts: It has taken longer [than](/ðən/) expected to adapt the scripts.

items.meaning: a situation in which something happens later than planned; to make something late

alerts.text: Acento en la segunda sílaba: «di-LÉI». El hispanohablante tiende a «DÉ-lei» por *demora*.
La primera sílaba es /ɪ/ breve, «di»; la segunda es el diptongo /eɪ/, «lei», no «le».
*A delay in*: «a-di-LÉI-in», la vocal final enlaza con *in* sin cortar.

example.speaker: helen
example.text: I understand there has been a delay in the data-export work.

items.meaning: a problem that reverses progress; to make something later

variants.label: Verb: set BACK
variants.speaker: coach
variants.text: The format change set us back two weeks.

alerts.text: Sustantivo: «SET-bak», acento delante. Verbo: «set BAK», acento en la partícula. El mismo patrón que *REcord / reCORD*.
La t de *set* delante de b se queda sin explosión: «se(t)-bak», nunca «sé-te-bak» con vocal añadida.
/æ/ de *back*: una a abierta que tira hacia la e, «bak». No es la a española pura.

example.speaker: ryan
example.text: The format change was a setback, but it hasn't pushed back the go-live date.

structures.title: Active cause, present consequence
structures.formula: have / has been + -ing (cause) + so / as a result + have / has + past participle (consequence)
structures.usage: The cause is still going on (continuous); the consequence is a present result (simple) or a present state.

structures.title: Linking cause and consequence
structures.formula: because of / due to / owing to + noun · because / since + clause · as a result / which is why + consequence
structures.usage: *Owing to* and *due to* are formal and take a noun phrase; *because* takes a full clause. *As a result* opens a sentence; *which is why* continues one.

examples.speaker: daniel
examples.text: {{Owing to}} a change in the data format, the delivery has been rescheduled.

examples.speaker: priya
examples.text: We're behind {{because}} we've been waiting for the supplier, {{which is why}} the date has moved.

l1.title: The cause in the present tense
l1.text: Spanish *es que estamos esperando desde el día 2* uses the present. English needs *we've been waiting since the 2nd*: the cause started in the past and continues.
l1.wrong: We are waiting for the data since the 2nd, so we are late.
l1.right: We've been waiting for the data since the 2nd, so we're late.

l1.title: Due to + a whole clause
l1.text: *Due to* and *owing to* take a noun phrase, not a clause. With a clause, use *because*.
l1.wrong: The module is late due to the supplier changed the format.
l1.right: The module is late due to a change in the supplier's format.

l1.title: Delay as «retrasarse»
l1.text: A project does not *delay*; it *is delayed* or *has slipped*. *Delay* as a verb needs an object (*delay the launch*).
l1.wrong: The reporting module has delayed two weeks.
l1.right: The reporting module has been delayed by two weeks.

l1.title: Naming the culprit
l1.text: Spanish allows a direct *la culpa es del proveedor*. In a client message, name the event, not the person, and never *guilty*, which belongs in court.
l1.wrong: The supplier is guilty of the delay.
l1.right: The delay is largely down to a change in the supplier's data format.

l1.title: For a deadline
l1.text: *Para el 6 de junio* is *by 6 June*, not *for*. *For* names a purpose or a recipient.
l1.wrong: We'll deliver the module for June 6.
l1.right: We'll deliver the module by June 6.

task.title: Explaining a delay to a client
task.scenario: You lead a small team. A piece of work your client is waiting for is going to be two weeks late: an external dependency (a supplier, another department, a legal review) has been slower than planned, and your own estimate was optimistic. Write the email that explains the delay, keeps the client's trust and proposes a revised date.
task.brief: Explain a delay diplomatically: the active cause, the consequence, what you have been doing in the meantime and a revised date.
steps: Open with the purpose: an update on one specific deliverable.
State that there has been a delay and give the active cause with *have been + -ing* and *since*.
Accept your share honestly (*partly*, *longer than expected*) without blaming a person.
Say what you have been doing in the meantime and what is not affected.
Give a revised date and your next contact.

extra.title: Extra: the formal line for the steering committee
extra.brief: Condense the delay into one formal sentence for a written report: the cause as a noun phrase, the passive, and what remains unchanged.

parts.speaker: alex
parts.text: Hi Tom, {{I'm writing to update you on}} the video tutorials for the help center. {{There has been a delay in}} the editing work: we{{'ve been waiting for}} the new brand guidelines {{since}} the 5th, and re-recording the voice-over {{has taken longer than expected}}, {{partly}} because our first estimate was optimistic. {{As a result}}, the tutorials {{have slipped}} from June 14 to June 28. {{In the meantime}}, we{{'ve been publishing}} the written articles, so the launch of the help center {{is not affected}}. I'll send you a {{revised}} schedule {{by Friday}} and flag it early if anything else changes. Best, Alex
parts.tts: Hi Tom, I'm writing to update you on the video tutorials for the help center. There has been a delay in the editing work: we've been waiting for the new brand guidelines since the fifth, and re-recording the voice-over has taken longer [than](/ðən/) expected, partly because our first estimate was optimistic. As a result, the tutorials have slipped from June fourteenth to June twenty-eighth. In the meantime, we've been publishing the written articles, so the launch of the help center is not affected. I'll send you a revised schedule by Friday and flag it early if anything else changes. Best, Alex
parts.label: Email to a client contact (neutral, professional)
notes: *There has been a delay in the editing work*: the delay is an event; nobody is named.
*We've been waiting for… since the 5th* (active cause) + *has taken longer than expected, partly because…* (honest share).
*As a result, the tutorials have slipped from… to…*: a consequence with real dates.
*In the meantime… is not affected*: what was done with the waiting time and what the client keeps.
*Revised schedule by Friday*: a delay with a plan attached.

parts.speaker: emma
parts.text: {{Owing to}} a change in the brand guidelines, delivery of the video tutorials {{has been rescheduled for}} 28 June; the launch date of the help center {{remains unchanged}}.
parts.tts: Owing to a change in the brand guidelines, delivery of the video tutorials has been rescheduled for the twenty-eighth of June; the launch date of the help center remains unchanged.
parts.label: Formal line for the steering committee (written)
notes: *Owing to* + noun phrase: the cause in four words, no story.
*Delivery… has been rescheduled for*: the passive and a noun (*delivery*) instead of *we will deliver*.
*Remains unchanged*: the reassuring fact goes last, so it is what the reader remembers.

selfCheck.text: ¿Tu correo explica la causa sin señalar a una persona (*there has been a delay in…*, *has been held up by…*)? ¿Qué frase concreta evita la culpa y cuál asume tu parte (*partly*)?
¿Está en el registro del cliente (*I'm writing to update you*, *revised date*), sin *hit a snag* ni *dragging their feet*? ¿Y la frase extra suena a informe (*owing to*, pasiva) y no a correo?
¿Pusiste la causa en presente (*we are waiting since*)? ¿*Due to* va seguido de un sustantivo y no de una oración? ¿*By* y no *for* con la fecha límite?
¿La causa activa va en *have been + -ing* y la consecuencia en *has + participio* o en pasiva (*has been delayed*)? ¿*Delay* lleva objeto o pasiva, nunca *the module has delayed*?
¿Diste una fecha nueva y un próximo contacto? Un retraso sin fecha nueva es una excusa; con fecha y plan, es gestión.
